> **What this case shows** — a simulator is only credible if it reproduces
> *reality*, not just if it looks plausible on synthetic data. Here the mechanistic
> **ECGSYN** dynamical model is validated against a **real** ECG (MIT-BIH record
> 100). Personalising ECGSYN's five P/Q/R/S/T event amplitudes to the real average
> beat raises the morphology correlation from **0.62** (generic model) to
> **0.905** (personalised), and — run at the real heart rate with the real HRV —
> the generator reproduces the **rate** (75.4 vs 75.3 bpm) and **HRV** (SDNN 46 vs
> 52 ms). This is the **validation-against-reality** tier, distinct from the
> synthetic-data parameter recovery that only *verifies* the estimator. **How to
> read it** — left, the real average beat with the generic and personalised ECGSYN
> beats overlaid; right, a strip of the personalised generator.

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — to validate a mechanistic generator against real data: build the
real **average beat** (and rate + HRV) from a recording, **personalise** the
model's parameters to it, then check the model reproduces the morphology, rate and
variability.
**Way of thinking** — "the simulator recovers its own parameters on synthetic
data" is **verification of the estimator**; "the simulator, fit to a subject,
reproduces that subject's real signal" is **validation of the model** — a
different, stronger claim, and the one that makes an in-silico experiment
trustworthy.
**Ecosystem usage** — `ecgsyn()` (PhysioTwin) as the cardiac generator; the same
personalise-then-predict protocol validates any twin against held-out real data.
:::

## Proposition

Personalised ECGSYN reproduces a real ECG: morphology correlation 0.62 → 0.905
after fitting the event amplitudes, with the generated rate (75.4 vs 75.3 bpm) and
HRV (SDNN 46 vs 52 ms) matching MIT-BIH record 100.

## Question & goal

**The question is model credibility, not code correctness.** A digital twin's
in-silico predictions are only worth trusting if the underlying simulator matches
reality. Parameter recovery on synthetic data (the twin generating its own truth)
verifies the *estimator*; it says nothing about whether the *model* is right. We
ask the harder question: fit the mechanistic ECGSYN model to a real subject and
see whether it reproduces that subject's actual ECG.

## Challenge & approach

We build the real average beat of MIT-BIH record 100 (2237 normal beats, lead
MLII, R-aligned and normalised), and its heart rate and HRV. We **personalise**
ECGSYN by fitting its five P/Q/R/S/T event amplitudes to the real beat, then drive
the personalised model at the real HR with the real HRV and compare the morphology,
rate and HRV.

## Data

**MIT-BIH record 100** (Moody & Mark, PhysioNet) — 2237 normal beats, lead MLII @
360 Hz. Details in [`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![The real average beat (blue) with the generic ECGSYN beat (grey dashed,
over-large P and T) and the personalised ECGSYN beat (red, tracking the real
P-QRS-T); right, a strip of the personalised generator at the matched rate and
HRV.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the generic model already has the right wave *ordering* but the
wrong wave *heights* (r = 0.62). Fitting the five event amplitudes — the cardiac
twin's personalisation — pulls the synthetic beat onto the real one (r = 0.905),
and the emergent rate and HRV match.

| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| morphology correlation, generic ECGSYN | 0.62 |
| morphology correlation, **personalised** | **0.905** |
| heart rate (synthetic vs real) | 75.4 vs **75.3** bpm |
| HRV SDNN (synthetic vs real) | 46 vs **52** ms |
| real beats used | 2237 |

## Conclusion

The mechanistic ECGSYN model, personalised to a real subject, reproduces that
subject's ECG morphology, rate and HRV — the model is **validated against
reality**, not merely verified on synthetic data. The transferable takeaway:
**separate verifying the estimator (synthetic recovery) from validating the model
(fit to a subject, reproduce their real signal) — only the latter licenses
in-silico prediction.**

## Open questions

- Fitting the event **angles and widths** (not only amplitudes), a **multi-lead /
  VCG** extension, and validation across **many records and leads** would raise the
  match and map the model's domain of applicability (including pathological beats).
  *Documented, not escalated.*

| step | function | package |

| coordination / rhythm generators | `kuramoto()` / `cpgMatsuoka()` | PhysioTwin |
| validity harness (V&V report) | `validateTwin()` | PhysioTwin |
